Question: What are your thoughts on the new Batman teaser?
Old_Answer: HOLY BONE-CRUNCHING BEATDOWN, BATMAN! The problem with a character like Batman is that he is just too mainstream. As such, every time there is a new iteration, people are quick to judge and condemn because they have their own unique tunnel vision of what the character should look and talk and move like. And these predispositions are mostly based on the recent incarnations of The Caped Crusader. The expectations from the actor as soon as their name is revealed are so high that the reality often falls short. It’s the most classic case of millions simultaneously judging the book by its cover. But here we are. And the naysayers have been proved wrong once more. What we have in the Batman trailer is a younger, inexperienced Batman who has still not come to terms with the death of his parents. We have a rookie vigilante who still needs to tell the thugs who he is, much like Bale in Batman Begins. We can see in Battinson’s eyes that he is not sure of what he is doing. And that he hasn’t been doing it for long. His Bruce Wayne lacks the confidence, the charm, the charisma. He is not a “playboy billionaire”, just an angry young man who seems like he hasn’t slept for months. What we are looking at is the rough draft for what will eventually become the world’s greatest hero and his rogue gallery. Matt Reeves confirmed so.[1] “It’s actually in a weird way the origins of a lot of our Rogues Gallery characters. Selina isn’t Catwoman yet, that’s actually part of the journey. And The Riddler is just emerging for the first time.” Farrell looks simply unrecognizable as Penguin. Catwoman is just a burglar with a woolen kitty-eaned full face mask. And that beatdown at the end, points to a far more Brutal Batman than we are accustomed to on the silver screen. Pattinson’s voice sounds amazing. Unlike Bale’s growl. The overall direction that Reeves is taking is amazing. We are finally getting a deranged, psychopathic Riddler played by the fabulous Paul Dano. Instead of just comedy shticks and giggles, this is a Riddler that will push the Dark Knight to the limits of his cognitive ability. Finally, a Batman who is just not cool gadgets and martial arts moves, but the world’s greatest detective skills. It’s long overdue that the casual fandom is reminded that the Riddler is a force to be reckoned with. That he deduced Batman’s identity but chose to not reveal it because “a riddle that everyone knows the answer to is worthless”. Finally, what a fantastic riddle to start off. I AM THE HYPE! Question: What are the worst coronavirus myths roaming around social media?
Old_Answer: One of the scariest things I have been reading all over is people pondering getting infected early. Yep. The “reasoning” seems to be two-fold: early infection will mean immunity later on when the virus is deadlier and the fact that they will get treated right now when the cases are low. But this is a very dangerous line of thinking. Firstly, there is NO evidence that like Chicken Pox, getting infected will build immunity to the virus. Secondly, the time-frame in which people get infected matters. In fact, one of the primary reasons that make COVID-19 so scary is the rate at which it is spreading. Worldwide, the infrastructure is not equipped to deal with such a sudden surge of patients that require utmost care and isolation — Coronavirus cases are pushing Italy's hospitals to the brink. The need of the hour is to “flatten the curve” — i.e. to slow down the spread of the virus so that the “peak number of cases at any point” remain low enough to be handled properly by our existing healthcare infrastructure. Washington Post has done a brilliant piece — https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/corona-simulator/ — providing simulations for multiple situations in a hypothetical town of 200 people. In essence, “JUST STAY HOME AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE, PEOPLE!”
Answer_with_writing_sample: The worst coronavirus myths circulating on social media are not just misleading; they pose a real threat to public health. One of the most pervasive myths is that COVID-19 is just like the flu and not particularly dangerous. This notion downplays the risks associated with a virus that has claimed millions of lives. The truth is, while both are respiratory infections, COVID-19 can lead to severe complications, especially in vulnerable populations. Another harmful myth is that masks are ineffective in preventing virus spread. This couldn’t be further from the truth; numerous studies have shown that masks significantly reduce transmission rates. Furthermore, the idea that only older individuals need to worry about COVID-19 is dangerously misguided. Young and seemingly healthy individuals can also experience severe outcomes, including long COVID. There are also myths around vaccines—claims that they alter DNA or contain microchips. These conspiracy theories are not based on any scientific evidence and only serve to erode public trust in essential health measures. Lastly, the notion that one can achieve immunity through natural exposure alone is reckless; the risks of long-term effects from actual infection far outweigh any potential benefits. We must collectively recognize these myths for what they are: misinformation that can cost lives. It’s crucial to rely on credible sources and scientific evidence to navigate through this pandemic. Social media can be a double-edged sword, but it’s our responsibility to combat false narratives and promote genuine information for the sake of public health and safety.

Question: What are some opinions about the new map of Nepal?
Old_Answer: The Indo-Nepal confrontation on the disputed areas in Uttarakhand and Sikkim is a tale as old as time. The current border demarcations have been in effect since the British Raj. Nepal is indeed right in claiming that “as part of the original Sugauli treaty, any region east of the Kali river is part of Nepal”. However, if we are to talk about and accept history then we should do it in its entirety. After the Treaty of Sugauli, there were more geographical changes done by the British. The issue here is that the Kali river originates somewhere in the middle. (See the tiny blue line) As you can see anything east of the river (except for the first couple of kms) is anyway part of Nepal. What Nepal is claiming now is that the portion north of the origin, and henceforth westward till Kuti village as part of Nepal. This again was addressed 200 years ago. To address this, in the 1830s, the British government clarified that the entire drainage area of the Kali river was part of British India. There is historical documentation to support this, and consequently, refute Nepal’s current claims. There is also an 1879 map that shows the frontier further to the east, following a ridge that runs down from near the Tinker Pass. Trade was a great obsession in the British colonial mind, and presumably Britain realigned the border to gain exclusive control over trade across the Lipu Lekh Pass and the traders using it. Whatever the sequence that led to this new border being imposed or agreed, or whatever date it occurred, maps prepared in Nepal during the Panchayat regime are identical to the post-1860 maps in showing the border as following the line of the river that flows down from below Lipu Lekh. Again, this indicated an acceptance, whether consciously or not, that the traditional trail to the pass fell exclusively on the Indian side and that the border agreed as part of the Sugauli Treaty was no longer valid. Also unhelpful to Nepal’s case is that the China-Nepal Boundary Treaty, formally signed by King Mahendra in Beijing on October 5, 1961 makes no reference at all to Lipu Lekh. The opening lines of Article 1 state: “The Chinese-Nepalese boundary line starts from the point where the watershed between the Kali River and the Tinkar River meet the watershed between the tributaries of the Mapchu (Karnali) River on the one hand and the Tinkar River on the other hand.” (Emphasis added.) This roughly corresponds to the border shown on the 1879 map and the one claimed by India today. The Nepal government published a map in 1960 with a similar boundary line. Article 3 of the China-Nepal Boundary Agreement of March 21, 1960, required the two countries to exchange maps and to set up a joint committee to start the process of delineation and demarcation. Presumably the map Nepal submitted was similar to the one openly published. In short, Nepal’s current claims hold no water. If we go far back, no present-day boundaries make sense. India could lay claim to Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar. But it doesn’t.

Question: What do you think about people who never wish to marry? Do you think they are doomed (since you are married)?
Old_Answer: There is a simple, singular thought-shift that could make the world a far more loving, encompassing place if everyone adopted it — the acceptance of personal choice. All of the 7.5 billion people on planet Earth should be absolutely free to choose what to do with their lives — the way they dress, their career choices, their lifestyle, and the philosophies they follow. With one simple caveat, of course — your actions and your choices should not be to the detriment of others. Speeding might give you an adrenaline boost, but it also endangers others on the road. It is ok to eat anything if there was no risk of it snowballing into a global pandemic. Eating endangered animals, similarly, adversely harms the overall ecosystem and might lead to the extinction of the said species. I am even ok with substance abuse, but then addicts often go on drug-fuelled rampages destroying lives and property. That is unacceptable. That said, the choice of partaking in the institution of marriage, thankfully, does not suffer from any such unintended consequences. As such, it should be absolutely no one’s business if someone decides to be a lifelong bachelor. Yes, there is the question of loneliness in old age. But again, most developed nations have a sturdy system of old-age homes where people can develop camaraderie in their twilight years. The concept of monogamous marriages is quite frankly outdated. We live in relatively far peaceful and prosperous times. The law can be reworked to take care of the legalities involving polygamy, polyandry, open relationships, and the entire multitude of possible domestic and amorous relationships. As we keep on evolving, we would need to make peace with a world order that changes rapidly and welcomes departures from the norm.
